articles.title: US citizen singer’s stay flagged in Agra over old Indian Aadhaar, missing Form C records
articles.summary: Indian singer turned US citizen reportedly visited India since 2022 without Form C filings; Agra hotel alerted FRRO, Aadhaar used, raising compliance and fee concerns.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: A prominent Indian singer who reportedly acquired US citizenship in 2022 had been travelling to India since then without his stays being reported through Form C, an official source said.During his latest visit to Agra, his stay was recorded through the form for the first time after FRRO officials stood firm on compliance. Hotel staff alerted the FRRO after the singer initially did not provide identification documents.The singer checked into a prominent Agra hotel between 4pm and 6pm on Monday, Oct 26, the source said. About three hours later, his Aadhaar was presented. Form C was submitted after Tuesday midnight, following the FRRO’s follow-up. The singer had checked out by then.According to the source, the singer said he had never filled Form C during his earlier visits to India. The Agra filing was the first time his stay had been reported through the form, the source said. Records confirming details of his previous visits were not available.The singer, a US citizen who was previously an Indian citizen, obtained US citizenship around 2022, the source said. He entered India through Mumbai on Monday on a business visa.The source said he was visiting for his scheduled performances in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and various other cities.A Bureau of Immigration notice clarifies that the accommodation provider must report every foreign national staying at its premises to the registration officer.The foreign guest is required to furnish the particulars requested by the provider. Under Rule 17, Form III, formerly Form C, must be submitted electronically within 24 hours of a foreign national’s check-in and check-out.The notice says the requirement applies regardless of the duration of stay and covers all foreign nationals, including OCI cardholders and minors.The notice also says a live photograph of each foreign guest should be taken at reception for identity verification and completion of Form III. It cites Sections 8(1) and 8(2) of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, concerning the respective duties of accommodation providers and foreign guests.Hotel staff alerted the FRRO, which followed up to ensure the form was filed. Under the rules, the accommodation provider is responsible for submitting it.The singer presented an Aadhaar obtained while he was an Indian citizen, sources said. A UIDAI official said Aadhaar establishes identity, not citizenship. Foreign nationals may apply for Aadhaar after residing in India for 182 days, with validity linked to their visa, the official said.“Since there is currently no provision requiring a person to surrender Aadhaar if their citizenship status changes, this US citizen has been misusing the Aadhaar for his benefit,” the official added.According to intelligence sleuths, the US singer visited an ASI-protected monument in Agra on Aadhaar issued when he was Indian citizen, therefore, he managed to avoid charges/fee which is levied on foreign nationals.Foreign tourists are charged Rs 1100, while domestic tourists are charged Rs 50.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: Netanyahu seeks 'right-wing, national, strong government' in tight Israel election race
articles.summary: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that his right-wing bloc secured a “clear, decisive majority” and called for a “right-wing,
articles.body: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that his right-wing bloc secured a “clear, decisive majority” and called for a “right-wing, national, strong government”, even as exit polls suggested that neither his camp nor the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot had secured the 61 seats required to form a majority in the 120-member Knesset.In his first reaction to the exit poll projections, Netanyahu addressed supporters at Likud’s election headquarters in Jerusalem, saying his party remained Israel’s largest political force and insisting that the right-wing bloc had enough support to govern.“What we’ve seen is that the Likud party is the largest party and nobody can compete with us,” he said. “The second thing that is clear as well is that the right block has a majority. And it is a decisive majority.”“We need to form a national right-wing government,” he added, arguing that Israel should not depend on Arab-led parties, which he described as being “against our existence”.Netanyahu also criticised television channels for projecting stronger results for opposition parties and accused them of discouraging his supporters from voting. He attacked what he called “criminal political investigations” into him.Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said Israel was facing a significant strategic opportunity alongside Washington.“Iran is weaker than ever, Israel is stronger than ever,” he said. “Israel is facing a historic, one-time opportunity along with our friend President Trump” to “remove the Iranian threat once and for all”.He also said, “We have been able to overcome our enemies, and we will be able to in the future.”The prime minister’s claims came after exit polls released by major Israeli television stations projected around 51 seats each for Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s camp, with Arab-led parties winning about 18 seats. The projections remain preliminary and could change as official counting progresses.The vote count has already begun. Once counting at polling stations is complete, officials will turn to the “double envelopes” - ballots cast by soldiers, diplomats, doctors and nurses who cannot leave their posts to vote in person. Around 600,000 such envelopes are in the count, and while they do not usually alter the overall outcome significantly, shifting exit polls have added to the uncertainty.Netanyahu’s Likud could emerge as the largest single party, but the broader political arithmetic leaves the formation of a government uncertain. His coalition, which previously had 68 members, had weakened over the past year amid disagreements, including over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.Eisenkot, meanwhile, said the exit polls indicated a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu and pledged to form a government.“Today, Israel went out to a referendum over the leadership that will lead Israel in the coming years,” he said. “The people decided in favor of change.”Promising “a new era — an era of hope”, Eisenkot warned Netanyahu not to “dare use Israel’s security for your political needs” while serving as caretaker prime minister.Turnout exceeded 77 per cent, the highest since 1999, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. The president will now be tasked with identifying the party leader best placed to assemble a governing coalition.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: HSBC CEO has a warning on data centers; says not all of them are 'good'; tells companies and investors: You have to look at …
articles.summary: HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery has warned against treating every data center equally.
articles.body: HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery has warned against treating every data center equally. He cautioned that companies and investors should review tenancy agreements, contract pricing, and the financial strength of individual projects before committing capital, even as artificial intelligence drives demand for new computing infrastructure. Elhedery described AI as a technology that could change how businesses operate, including HSBC. However, he argued that confidence in AI’s prospects should not translate into indiscriminate data center investment. Speaking to CNBC, Elhedery said “One has to be selective. You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging.”His warning comes as technology companies borrow heavily to build facilities, increasing concerns about project quality, debt levels and whether future demand will support the contracts behind each development.What the HSBC CEO told investors to examineElhedery said AI could boost productivity and change how employees work, but he took a more cautious position on the infrastructure supporting the technology. Data centers house the servers used for AI systems and cloud computing, and their financial performance often depends on long-term agreements with tenants.“It’s going to put a lot of power back in the hands of our colleagues because of the level of productivity it gives them, so it’s going to be transformational, and we’re certainly very much on a journey to adopt it,” he said, adding that AI would help to “re-engineer the bank.”Why data center financing is under scrutinyHSBC is directly exposed to the sector as a financier and as a data center operator. For example, in its 2025 annual report, the bank cited data centers and AI as transition-related industries it supports.Investment in the sector has accelerated as companies compete for computing capacity. McKinsey estimates that worldwide data center spending could reach $7 trillion by 2030.A growing part of that expansion is expected to rely on borrowing. JPMorgan estimated that by the end of the decade, $4.1 trillion of the projected AI infrastructure financing could come from debt.The borrowing is also adding pressure to bond markets. Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic adviser at Allianz, said large technology companies were competing with governments for financing.“Governments are borrowing what they’re borrowing, plus they’re refinancing debt at a higher level of rates,” he said. ”[And] you have hyperscalers who last year raised $200 billion in bond financing, and are probably going to raise a trillion in bond financing this year. They are yield-insensitive. They are spread-insensitive because they are betting on something that is truly transformational.”​You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Karnataka MLC polls: Big setback for DK Shivakumar as BJP-led NDA wins all 4 seats
articles.summary: BENGALURU: In a major setback to the ruling Congress and chief minister D K Shivakumar, the BJP-led NDA won all four Karnataka Legislative Council seats
articles.body: BENGALURU: In a major setback to the ruling Congress and chief minister D K Shivakumar, the BJP-led NDA won all four Karnataka Legislative Council seats that went to polls on October 23, sweeping both teachers’ and graduates’ constituencies.The NDA fielded three BJP candidates and one JD(S) candidate.JD(S) candidate A P Ranganath defeated Congress veteran and five-time MLC Puttanna in the Bengaluru Teachers’ constituency, while BJP candidate Shashil G Namoshi registered his fifth victory in the North-East Teachers’ constituency, defeating Congress nominee Sharanappa Mattur by 3,297 votes. Namoshi secured 15,596 first-preference votes against Mattur’s 12,299.Counting concluded at Kalaburagi, where around 30,253 voters had exercised their franchise. Of the votes counted, 28,380 were valid, while 1,873 were rejected.In the graduates’ constituencies, BJP candidates SV Sankanur and KM Suresh also emerged victorious, completing the NDA’s clean sweep of all four seats.In the West Graduates’ constituency, Sankanur secured his third consecutive victory, defeating Congress rival Mohan Limbikai. In the other graduates’ constituency, BJP candidate KM Suresh won the seat, ensuring that the NDA did not concede any ground to the ruling party in the elections.This is the second biennial legislative council election since Shivakumar became chief minister on June 3. In the June 18 elections to seven council seats from the MLAs’ quota, Congress won five seats and the BJP secured two. However, the ruling party failed to replicate that performance in the teachers’ and graduates’ constituencies.Ranganath won the Bengaluru Teachers’ constituency on his third attempt, defeating Puttanna by 908 votes. He secured 10,810 first-preference votes against Puttanna’s 9,902.Ranganath had lost to Puttanna in the 2022 and 2024 elections. This time, he capitalised on a sympathy wave to secure victory. articles.title: In 2020, MacKenzie Scott gave $10 million to a South Carolina charity; six years later, part of that gift is helping turn a rundown Columbia motel site into 30 affordable homes for local families
articles.summary: Six years after philanthropist and ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, MacKenzie Scott donated $10 million to a South Carolina charity; part of that
articles.body: Six years after philanthropist and ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, MacKenzie Scott donated $10 million to a South Carolina charity; part of that money is now helping fund affordable housing in Columbia. As part of the project, a former motel site is being redeveloped into 30 rental homes for families with different income levels. The $12.8 million project, called Grand Village, is being developed by nonprofit Homeless No More, which began construction with a groundbreaking ceremony on October 13.According to the organisation's official website, the site was once occupied by the Grand Motel, a property dating back to the 1950s at the corner of Two Notch Road and West Beltline Boulevard. Over the years, its condition had deteriorated. The new development will replace much of the old property, although two existing two-storey buildings will be renovated. The motel's historic sign will also be retained.For families looking for affordable accommodation, the development will offer one, two and three-bedroom rental homes. Some of these are intended for households with very low incomes, while others will be available to working residents, including teachers and firefighters.This comes as South Carolina faces a wider housing problem. According to South Carolina Public Radio, Homeless No More President and CEO Lila Anna Sauls said nearly half of renters in the state spend more than 30% of their household income on housing. With accommodation becoming difficult to afford, the organisation hopes Grand Village will provide another option for families who need reasonably priced homes.How will MacKenzie Scott's donation be used?In 2020, Scott gave $10 million to United Way of the Midlands. Grand Village is the first local project to receive funding from that contribution, according to the charity's president and CEO, Sara Fawcett.The $12.8 million budget is being supported by several organisations, including the South Carolina State Housing Finance and Development Authority, Richland County and the SC Community Loan Fund. Other partners include Dominion Energy, First Citizens Bank and the Central Carolina Community Foundation.The decision to retain and renovate some of the existing motel buildings also played a role in securing financial support. Officials said the combination of new construction and renovation allowed the state housing authority to obtain $11 million from two funding programmes.How families will qualify for the affordable homesAccording to Sauls, some units will serve households earning around 30% of the area's median income. Other units will be intended for those earning approximately 50%, 70% or 80%. This approach allows the development to accommodate families with different financial circumstances.State Senator Tameika Isaac Devine raised the issue during the groundbreaking ceremony. She said the state's growing population had increased the need to ensure that people could afford to live near their workplaces.Devine also spoke about possible government action, including discussions around zoning rules, building regulations and ways to increase housing availability.What will happen to the rest of the motel property?Grand Village will include facilities for the surrounding neighbourhood. A new community centre will provide space for local events, after-school activities and mentoring programmes for children. It will be named the James E Christopher Community Center in memory of Jim Christopher, a former Homeless No More board member who supported the development before he died in 2023.The centre could be particularly useful for people living in the neighbouring Belvedere community. Its community organisation currently holds meetings at a water treatment facility, according to its president, Diane Wiley.Grand Village moves towards completionConstruction of the 30 homes is expected to take around 12 months. Sauls said the community centre could take another four to six months to finish.Grand Village is part of a longer effort by Homeless No More to help families find stable accommodation. The nonprofit already operates emergency and transitional housing services and began developing affordable homes for working families in 2015.It has since built dozens of housing units along the Two Notch Road corridor. The organisation is also working on additional projects, including a former hotel property in Lexington County, Edgewood Village and Andrew's Village.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A self-taught Birmingham teenager built a gesture-controlled robotic hand for about £30; the invention attracted 2.6 million views and requests from students worldwide
articles.summary: A self-taught teenager from Birmingham has attracted 2.6 million views on TikTok after building a gesture-controlled robotic hand for about £30.
articles.body: A self-taught teenager from Birmingham has attracted 2.6 million views on TikTok after building a gesture-controlled robotic hand for about £30. Suleymaan Khan, 17, developed the device using camera recognition and code he wrote himself, with materials including foamboard, card and hot glue. According to Hyphen, hundreds of people have contacted him to learn how to recreate the invention, while students around the world have sought his advice on robotics projects. Khan is now working on step-by-step kits to help others build the hand, alongside developing further robotic inventions.How does Khan’s £30 gesture-controlled robotic hand workKhan's latest robotic hand is fully articulated and controlled through gestures. It uses camera recognition, supported by code that he wrote himself. The project demonstrates how he has progressed from simple homemade constructions to more complex robotic systems. Unlike his early cardboard creations, the hand combines physical components with programming to respond to recognised movements. The invention has attracted attention because Khan developed it using inexpensive, readily available materials rather than relying on costly specialist equipment.The cost of the project was approximately £30, according to Hyphen. Foamboard, card and hot glue were among the materials used to construct the hand. Its relatively low cost has prompted hundreds of people to ask Khan how to build a similar device themselves. He told the publication that he was working on putting together step-by-step kits to help people recreate the invention. The planned kits reflect the interest generated by the project and the requests he has received from people wanting to learn how the robotic hand works.Khan’s robotics projects attract followers on YouTube and TikTokKhan's robotics projects have developed a following on social media, where his work has reached audiences interested in technology and engineering. Hyphen reported that he had more than 400,000 likes and 20,000 followers across YouTube and TikTok. The robotic hand alone received 2.6 million views on TikTok. Alongside this online attention, students from different countries have approached him for help with their own robotics work, including university assignments and projects that they have struggled to complete.Khan described how students in Dubai contacted him shortly before his interview with Hyphen, seeking advice about a university assignment involving a robot. He has increasingly made helping other people an important part of his work. Reflecting on his development as an inventor, he said, “It’s cool to see where I started”. His experience illustrates how online platforms have enabled a young robotics enthusiast to share his projects with an international audience and connect with learners seeking practical technical guidance.How did Khan build the Pepper humanoid robot at the age of 12Before developing the gesture-controlled hand, Khan built several other projects, including remote-controlled paper planes and a humanoid robot called Pepper. He created Pepper when he was 12, using LEGO Mindstorms, cardboard and dental floss. The robot could move around, pick up and carry objects in its arms, and use motion sensors in its eyes to help prevent collisions. Although Pepper is now damaged and can no longer stand independently, the project helped Khan learn how to build more complex machines while working with limited resources.Pepper also earned Khan the 2023 Network Rail national innovation award at the Big Bang Fair, a UK science and engineering competition for young people aged 11 to 18, according to Hyphen. He has since secured an apprenticeship at a local robotics company while continuing to develop his own creations in his spare time. His next project is another humanoid robot that he hopes will incorporate artificial intelligence for speech recognition, object recognition and home mapping. Khan has also expressed an interest in developing prosthetics in the future, identifying their cost as an area he would like to address through his work.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan pledged a donation of $50 million to Sacramento State University.
articles.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan pledged a donation of $50 million to Sacramento State University. The gift from Zuckerberg and Chan was aimed to fund abatement, demolition and initial construction of a new downtown campus, Fortune reports. The donation came just weeks after the couple announced a major shift in the focus of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), directing most of its philanthropic efforts toward biomedical AI research and scientific discovery. The move signals a broader strategy that mirrors Zuckerberg's aggressive push into AI both at Meta and through the family's charitable ventures. California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the gift on January 28 and tied it to a redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento’s Capitol Mall. The money, from Zuckerberg and Meta, will make room for new student housing alongside academic space, including state-of-the-art STEM labs and an AI center.Zuckerberg also said that the investments will help strengthen communities and support the upcoming generation of leaders and innovators. Newsom added that this gift from the couple will enable the school keep building its pipeline of tech talent, and that students need to be able to afford to live where they study.Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan gave $50 million for Sacramento redevelopmentEarlier this year, California Governor Gavin Newsom unveiled a $50 million gift from Zuckerberg and Meta tied to the redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento's Capitol Mall. As reported by Fortune, the funding made by Meta CEO and his wife will help support the abatement, demolition and initial construction work for a new downtown campus of Sacramento State University. The project is also said to include student housing, STEM-focused academic facilities along with a dedicated AI centre.Newsom further added that the investment would also lead to encourage the students for technology-related careers and will also take care of the housing needs at the same time. The donation made by Zuckerberg and Chan also comes at a time when California is debating over the proposed billionaire tax. The state is proposing to impose one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires which has led to the exit of many high-profile and wealthy residents from the state. The report noted that Zuckerberg has not publicly commented on the proposal and continues to invest heavily in California through both business and philanthropic initiatives.The philanthropic shiftThe gift comes after Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, announced late last year that they would move most of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) toward AI-powered biomedical research. The initiative launched in 2015 with a pledge to give away 99 percent of the couple’s fortune. It has since moved away from its original focus on education and social justice, though the couple say they will continue to make other local donations.Biohub, a growing network of biomedical research institutes, is the centrepiece. The couple say it aims to cure or prevent all disease. At an event at the Biohub Imaging Institute in Redwood City in November, reported by the Associated Press, Zuckerberg said the Biohub model has been the most impactful thing they have done and that it will be the main focus of their philanthropy going forward.The refocus has had a cost. CZI recently laid off 70 staff, mostly at its Redwood City headquarters in San Mateo County. Fortune argues that the Sacramento AI center follows the same playbook, funding infrastructure for training AI talent, similar to Biohub’s shared research tools, rather than one-off scholarships or small, incremental gifts.California’s 5% tax on billionairesThe donation also arrives as California considers a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth. Fortune notes that several prominent billionaires, including Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Craft Ventures’ David Sacks, have already moved their permanent residences out of state to avoid it. Zuckerberg has made no public statement about the tax and is instead putting more money into California. He owns a compound of 11 properties in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighbourhood, valued at more than $110 million, and Meta has a 57-acre headquarters campus nearby, plus more than 400,000 square feet of office space in Menlo Park.Meta's AI ambitionsFortune sees a common thread between Zuckerberg’s business and his giving. Meta has committed to spending between $115 billion and $135 billion on building “superintelligent” agents for feeds, ads and commerce, and the Sacramento gift helps build the talent pipeline for such jobs. Biohub, meanwhile, is focused on “frontier AI” and “frontier biology,” using large-scale models for virtual cells, immune reprogramming and disease prediction. In a November blog post, Zuckerberg and Chan wrote that they are very excited about the decade ahead and expect challenges as well as progress toward some of humanity’s long-term dreams.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, conservation teams began removing invasive rats and pigs from a Pacific island; by 2026, native forests were regenerating, rare birds were nesting and sea turtles had returned after decades
articles.summary: A remote island in Samoa is showing signs of ecological recovery after conservation teams removed invasive rats and feral pigs that had threatened its
articles.body: A remote island in Samoa is showing signs of ecological recovery after conservation teams removed invasive rats and feral pigs that had threatened its native wildlife and vegetation. According to a report published by Island Conservation⁠ on October 20, 2026, Nu’utele Island has begun recovering its native forests, while rare birds are breeding and sea turtles have returned to nest after decades of absence. Updates from the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP)⁠ and Good News Network⁠ also highlight the conservation effort and its early benefits. Located off the eastern coast of Upolu, Samoa’s most populous island, Nu’utele lies within a marine protected area and is recognised as a Key Biodiversity Area. Its largely intact tropical forest provides habitat for native plants, birds and other wildlife, including species that have become increasingly vulnerable elsewhere in the region.However, invasive rats and feral pigs had disrupted the island’s ecological balance. Rats threaten bird populations by preying on eggs and chicks, while pigs disturb the soil, damage vegetation and prevent young plants from establishing themselves. Their combined impact had weakened the island’s ability to sustain wildlife and regenerate naturally.The restoration initiative, led by Samoa’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment in partnership with Island Conservation, SPREP’s Pacific Regional Invasive Species Management Support Service (PRISMSS) and local communities, sought to reverse that damage by removing the invasive animals. Between March 2025 and May 2026, teams conducted 12 expeditions and spent more than 130 days working across the island’s difficult terrain. Local landowners and community members from Aleipata also participated in the effort, which was supported through the regional Predator Free Pacific programme.The first signs of recovery have emerged across the forest floor and coastal habitats. Native seedlings are growing in areas where regeneration had previously been suppressed, offering evidence that the removal of invasive animals is allowing natural processes to resume. The improvements are also benefiting local food production. A family on the island has been able to grow bananas, pineapples, papayas and taro, while giant taro plants are thriving in areas where crops had previously struggled. The results suggest that restoring native ecosystems can support both biodiversity and the livelihoods of communities that depend on the land.Wildlife surveys have produced particularly encouraging findings. Researchers recorded several active nests containing eggs belonging to the Shy Ground Dove, a species whose population has declined across the Southwest Pacific. Nu’utele holds Samoa’s largest remaining population of the bird. Surveys also identified a nest belonging to the endemic Samoan Starling, alongside breeding activity among other native birds, including the Samoan Flycatcher and Samoan Whistler. The findings suggest that removing invasive predators has improved conditions for birds to reproduce successfully.Sea turtles have also returned to nest after decades of absence, marking another important development for the island’s coastal wildlife. Conservationists recorded a land crab species not previously documented on Nu’utele, while researchers expect crab populations to benefit as pressure from invasive predators declines. Land crabs play an important role in island ecosystems by moving nutrients between forests, reefs and the surrounding ocean. Their recovery could therefore have benefits beyond the immediate shoreline, helping maintain ecological connections within the marine protected area.The restoration could also create opportunities to protect threatened species in the future. With invasive rats and pigs removed, Nu’utele may provide a safer refuge for the Mao, a threatened native Samoan forest bird affected by habitat loss, invasive species and extreme weather. Plans to establish a new population of the species form part of Island Conservation’s wider Pacific restoration programme for 2026 to 2032.Beyond wildlife recovery, healthier forests can strengthen the island’s ability to withstand climate impacts. Native vegetation helps anchor soil, limit erosion and retain water, while supporting the biodiversity that keeps ecosystems functioning. These natural benefits are increasingly important across the Pacific, where communities face stronger storms and changing rainfall patterns.The early results from Nu’utele demonstrate how coordinated conservation efforts can help restore damaged island ecosystems. Continued monitoring will be needed to determine how wildlife populations, forest regeneration and coastal habitats develop over time, but the return of nesting turtles, breeding birds and native vegetation offers encouraging evidence that the island is moving towards recovery.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2010, a Texas father opened an accessible theme park inspired by his daughter; Morgan’s Wonderland has since welcomed more than 3.8 million guests from 50 states and 123 countries
articles.summary: Discover how Morgan's Wonderland, the world's first ultra-accessible theme park founded by Gordon Hartman, has transformed the experience for disabled visitors, welcoming millions from around the globe since 2010.
articles.body: Many mainstream theme parks emphasize thrill, capacity and spectacle, features that can create barriers for some disabled visitors. For families with a child who uses a wheelchair, is sensitive to sound, or cannot speak, a theme-park visit can become an organizational challenge. Although there are arrangements at the parks to accommodate such visitors, there is usually nothing that is pre-planned according to their requirements. In San Antonio, Texas, one individual decided to create something new by considering the opposite approach. As a homebuilder rather than an amusement-park operator, he drew inspiration from a deeply personal experience. Namely, he saw how his daughter was excluded from the playground. This experience led him to create a playground designed for everyone.From a foundation in 2005 to opening day on April 10, 2010The Gordon Hartman Foundation was established in 2005 by Gordon Hartman, a former real estate developer, to assist people with disabilities, Gulf News reports. In 2007, after realizing that other children often avoided Morgan because she could not speak, Gordon decided to create an inclusive park. Morgan’s biography of Hartman says that Morgan’s Wonderland opened on April 10, 2010, as the world’s first Ultra-Accessible theme park and the park’s own account puts the journey from the 2007 decision to opening day at 39 months. Hartman thought that families like his required a space that was less bustling than the traditional parks but was not sure that people were going to show up.A 25-acre park with a core of 25 attractions and free entry for guests with a disabilityThe park covers 25 acres and Morgan’s 2024 press release describes a core of 25 attractions that existed before the expansion. In 2024, Morgan’s Wonderland unveiled the largest expansion since its 2010 opening and Visit San Antonio’s release on the plan covers the four new attractions. A report carried by Intergame Online says the park caps daily attendance so it never gets too loud or the lines too long and admission is free for guests with special needs. Morgan’s March 2024 press release put the expansion at $6.5 million, while the plan announced the previous October had estimated $6 million, a figure Blooloop repeated. Morgan’s Wonderland’s 2024 announcement lists the four new attractions as the 4D Magic Cinema, Pirate’s Island Cruises, Rocket’s Sky Flight Adventure, which is a four-seat zip line and Jette’s Magic Bikes. According to Health Club Management, the Magic Cinema uses electric actuator-based motion effects, which can be disabled for guests who do not want motion effects.From 1.6 million guests in the first decade to more than 3.8 million todayThe family travel site Taking the Kids reported that more than 1.6 million guests from 50 states and 73 countries had visited the park during its first decade. During the 2024 expansion announcement, Hartman cited the figure as 2.7 million guests from 50 states and more than 120 countries. The park’s website currently reports more than 3.8 million guests over 16 years of operation, from 50 states and 123 countries. The number of countries represented has risen from 73 to 123, while total attendance has more than doubled.What a 2023 review of 14 playground auditing tools foundThe wider research context helps explain why a park like this stands out. A 2023 paper in Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences, A Scoping Review of Tools to Evaluate Existing Playgrounds for Inclusivity of Children with Disabilities, was led by Leah G. Taylor. The authors also draw attention to the fact that there are almost 240 million children who suffer from disabilities throughout the world and have problems properly participating in society. In the 2023 scoping review, there were 14 resources from both academic and grey literature on playground auditing tools found. The team synthesized features of those tools into 13 recommendations for inclusive playground design. Just two tools covered 12 of those 13 recommendations and the tools applied the notion of inclusion differently, mostly in terms of physical inclusion.The paper also notes that most of the tools were at an early stage of development and few had been formally tested for reliability and validity. Most of the tools also paid little attention to sensory, social and communication barriers. For its part, the park’s biography says it was not meant to be a separate place for people with disabilities, but a place where disabled and non-disabled visitors could share the same rides.A 2022 observation study and the 71% active play figureA second paper, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, looked at how children actually behave in an inclusive setting. The study, Children’s Usage of Inclusive Playgrounds: A Naturalistic Observation Study of Play, used two trained observers and a modified version of the System for Observing Play and Recreation in Children tool at a playground built for all ages and abilities. The study also found that 71% of the children observed were engaged in active play. Moreover, it should be noted that there were children without disabilities who seemed to be attracted to the playground. Both papers discuss further research into the interactions between the children with disabilities and playgrounds. The study observed not only the children’s activity but also their interactions and found that most were social or parallel rather than solitary. Nevertheless, neither of these two papers considered Morgan's Wonderland directly; instead, they create the background for the park. In the study of the auditing tool discussed above, it is stated that every space should be audited in regard to its current capabilities and shortcomings. It is true for every inclusive park.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Process becomes punishment in our system': Ex-SC judge Sanjay Kaul on Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam bail pleas
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Sanjay Kishan Kaul has said that the period before conviction or acquittal has become a \"punishment\" in India,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Sanjay Kishan Kaul has said that the period before conviction or acquittal has become a "punishment" in India, commenting on the denial of bail to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. He said that prolonged legal proceedings can themselves become a form of punishment and that bail should generally be the norm.In an interview with news agency ANI, Kaul said he had generally taken a liberal view on bail, but acknowledged that certain laws explicitly restrict the granting of bail in specific cases."I have taken a generally very liberal view on bail. I feel the bail cannot be the punishment. The conviction is the punishment. In our system, unfortunately, the pre-conviction or acquittal period itself becomes a punishment. The process becomes a punishment," former Supreme Court judge said.Kaul said several judges had raised concerns about the issue. He also referred to a judgment written by Justice Sundaresh, with whom he had dealt with the question of bail and the principles governing custody."And many judges have been writing and talking about it. In fact, I, sitting with Justice Sundaresh, had dealt elaborately with the bail itself, trying to say, why are you people under custody? Justice Sundaresh wrote the judgment. He's, to my mind, a liberal judge on this. And we tried to lay down norms, etc., which were already in existence, but trying to, you know, until this case. So in most cases, our view is, that bail should be the norm. But there are certain acts which prohibit bail," said Kaul.Kaul has co-authored an upcoming memoir, Without Fear or Favour, with Jay Vinayak Ojha. The book is scheduled for release on October 31.Khalid and Imam are accused under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in connection with an alleged larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots. According to the prosecution, the violence left 53 people dead and more than 700 injured.The riots broke out amid protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, and the proposed National Register of Citizens.On January 5 this year, the Supreme Court denied bail to Khalid and Imam in the case related to the alleged conspiracy behind the 2020 riots. In its judgment, the court observed that the two accused stood on a "qualitatively different footing" in terms of the prosecution's case and the evidence against them.In September, the Delhi high court had also rejected their bail pleas. The case stems from FIR 59/2020, registered by the Delhi Police Special Cell to investigate the alleged larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots.‘Met him only a couple of times’: Justice Kaul on Saurav DasMeanwhile, former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul also clarified his association with Cockroach Janta Party activist Saurav Das, saying he had met him only a couple of times when Das was working as a journalist and had advised him to "taper down a little" in his language.Justice Kaul told news agency ANI that a photograph of him with Das, taken at a Diwali gathering about a year ago, was being used to suggest that he shared a particular ideology."So, it was one year ago. He was not even in the news then," Justice Kaul said, explaining how the meeting came about."He was a journalist, maybe met me a couple of times. He was insistent that I must, at Diwali time, come. I was going somewhere else. I said, 'Okay, I'll drop in for ten minutes.' I told my wife, 'Have a cup of coffee, I'll drop in for ten minutes, and then we'll go.' That's all that happened," he said.Asked whether he had mentored Das at any point, Justice Kaul denied doing so, while acknowledging that he had advised the activist on his choice of words."I was not mentoring him, but once or twice he met me, I told him that, I will always tell you to taper down a little in your language," he said.Justice Kaul added that differences in language and expression across generations could sometimes cause discomfort, particularly among those accustomed to more civil forms of conversation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1964, an Oregon father began hand-building a fairy-tale park after a family road trip; Enchanted Forest opened in 1971 and now draws more than 100,000 visitors a year
articles.summary: Discover the enchanting story of the Enchanted Forest in Oregon, a fairy-tale park built by Roger Tofte that has captivated over 100,000 visitors annually since its opening in 1971. Learn about its origins, whimsical sculptures, and the legacy of the Tofte family.
articles.body: Beside a major interstate in Oregon, a castle-shaped road sign topped by a nursery rhyme character marks the exit for a family-run theme park. Drivers who take the exit find a wooded hillside with shaded paths and along those paths sit hand-built figures from fairy tales and nursery rhymes, along with later additions such as rides and a western-themed town. Unlike the large corporate parks, it began as the spare-time project of a single state employee who built many of the early figures by hand and it is still owned and run by the same family.A 1963 family road trip, a $500 down payment and 20 acres bought in 1964NPR traces the park’s origin to a 1963 family road trip. Roger Tofte was a draftsman for the Oregon State Highway Division and returned home wanting to build something more ambitious. Tofte and his wife Mavis bought twenty wooded acres in 1964 for $4,000, the Oregon Encyclopedia records and NPR reports that the down payment was $500. The Spaces Archives note that his only previous cement project was a small backyard swimming pool. He worked on evenings and weekends and his coworkers at the Highway Department nicknamed the site “Idiot Hill,” though several of them ended up helping him, the Oregon Encyclopedia says.Opening day on August 8, 1971: 75 visitors, then 1,000 a week laterConstruction began in 1964 and the park opened to the public in 1971, about seven years later, KOIN reported. Tofte sculpted fairy tale and nursery rhyme characters such as Peter Peter Pumpkin Eater, the Seven Dwarfs and Little Red Riding Hood, as NPR described and his first sculpture was the castle at the entrance to Storybook Lane. As opening approached, the family had run out of money and still needed $2,000 to finish the park and at the last minute, Tofte borrowed the funds from a second bank, according to the Spaces Archives records.The park opened on August 8, 1971. Seventy-five people visited that day, according to NPR, paying one dollar for adults and 50 cents for children and by the following Sunday, after a front-page article in the local paper, roughly 1,000 visitors came through the gates. The staff included Roger, Mavis and their children Susan, Ken, Mary and Lori, the Oregon Encyclopedia notes. Tofte quit his highway department job in 1973.More than 100,000 visitors a year and three generations of the Tofte familyThe park operates from March to September and employs three generations of the Tofte family. The Oregon Encyclopedia puts annual attendance above 100,000, a figure NPR also attributed to the Tofte family in 2018, while the Spaces Archives lists up to 200,000. Nature too has not spared the place. During the winter of 1990, a storm toppled 20 trees and caused extensive damage to Ice Mountain Bobsled. In 2009, another ice storm brought down more trees. In 2014, two visitors trying to take a photograph caused the Humpty Dumpty statue to fall. Tofte continued building and developing the amusement park over several decades. OPB reported that he died on February 13, 2026, at age 96.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Virginia family’s land held a 200-year-old dam once used by a five-story grain mill; removal reopened 30 miles of stream, and mussel beds began returning
articles.summary: The removal of a 200-year-old dam in southwest Virginia has reopened over 30 miles of stream, allowing endangered mussel species to return and restoring a vital ecosystem. Discover the benefits and implications of this significant environmental project led by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
articles.body: Old mill dams are easy to overlook on farmland. Often, they linger on private property long after the mill they were built for is gone. The people who live near them may never consider their effect on the river. In southwest Virginia, there was such a dam on one family’s farm. The mill it once powered had been long gone, but the dam and its effect on the river system remained.A dam and five-story mill built between 1818 and 1834 on the Bowen family’s landThe US Fish and Wildlife Service reported that the Bowen family has been tied to its land at Maiden Spring, Virginia, for about 250 years, or seven generations by the Service’s count. The ancestors first inhabited the area during the 1760s near a spring that feeds a creek into the Little River, which is a major tributary of the Clinch River. The Little River was dammed somewhere between 1818 and 1834, with a five-story mill being erected to process the grains produced at the settlement. The mill was later torn down, but the dam, 130 feet wide and 14 feet tall, survived. The family had long been good stewards of the land, planting native trees near the water and fencing cattle out of the river. However, the three Bowen brothers, who currently operate the family farm, were unaware of the fact that the disused dam was hindering certain fish and mussel species.A river system with 46 mussel species, 20 of them endangeredThe Service describes the Clinch River system as one of the most ecologically valuable and diverse freshwater areas in North America, home to 100 fish species, five of them threatened or endangered and 46 freshwater mussel species, 20 of them endangered. The river also hosts the largest concentration of federally protected species in the United States. Corey Kanuckel, a Service biologist with the Partners for Fish and Wildlife office in Virginia, approached the brothers about the dam. Surveys found no mussels above the dam in the channel or within 200 meters of its base. Kanuckel named several species affected by the dam: the Cumberland moccasinshell and Tennessee clubshell, both at-risk species, the listed slabside pearlymussel and the Tennessee pigtoe, which the Service’s 2024 story says is proposed for the endangered species list.A $200,000 grant, a notching phase and more than 30 miles of stream The brothers accepted removal in exchange for a promise from the Service to restore the property in a better state and an added benefit that removal would reduce a hazard and liability. Gravel was provided by the Service to make sure that heavily used sections of the land were stabilized, allowing farm lanes to remain accessible. The US Fish and Wildlife Service awarded the Canaan Valley Institute $200,000 through the National Fish Passage Program, which received funding under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, for the Little River Dam removal project, according to the Service’s April 2024 story.Notches were first cut into the dam to allow passage of water without bringing too much sediment, followed by the removal of the remaining dam and restoration of the streambank. The Service’s April 2024 story said the removal was complete and had opened 30 miles of stream, with bank stabilization under way and due to finish in summer 2024. The Service also reported promising mussel bed development downstream. Its project page is less consistent on mileage: the summary says over 30 miles, while the Quick Facts table lists 50 stream miles reconnected. The page does not explain the difference.A 2007 USGS report on host fish and mussels in the Neversink RiverA US Geological Survey report, Relations of Environmental Factors with Mussel-Species Richness in the Neversink River, New York, describes a 6-year study of seven mussel species. It notes that mussel larvae develop in species-specific host fish, so impoundments that block those fish also limit where mussels can live. Removing the Cuddebackville Dam gave diadromous and other fish that host rare mussels access to habitat they could not reach before. From 1997 to 2002, the team sampled 28 sites across the river and its tributaries, then built a model linking mussel richness to 10 environmental variables, including elevation, drainage area, channel width, sand content, velocity, shear stress, ANC and calcium, phosphorus and sulfate concentrations. The endangered dwarf wedgemussel and threatened swollen wedgemussel occurred alongside five other species.A four-year study of small dam removal on North Carolina’s Deep RiverA 2013 paper in Walkerana, Short-term effects of small dam removal on freshwater mussel assemblage, tracked mussels for four years after a small hydropower dam came out of North Carolina’s Deep River in 2006. Its before-after-control-impact analyses showed no significant change in mussel density or species richness at the tailrace or the drained impoundment and stranding in the dewatered reservoir caused little mortality. The authors monitored two impact sites and two reference sites each year, using transect surveys and quadrat excavation to track density, richness and survival. Apparent annual survival of Eastern Elliptio at the tailrace did not differ from control sites. They concluded that careful planning, timing and method can limit short-term harm. Neither study looked at the Little River, but together they show why removing a dam matters for mussels and what removal can do to the mussels already living below it. The Service says the mussel beds downstream are still in an early stage of recovery.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two spans of a 140-year-old Scottish railway bridge fell into the River Spey; engineers are investigating the collapse as restoration options could cost more than £1 million
articles.summary: Two spans of a 140-year-old railway bridge have collapsed into the River Spey in north-east Scotland, leaving engineers investigating the damage and
articles.body: Two spans of a 140-year-old railway bridge have collapsed into the River Spey in north-east Scotland, leaving engineers investigating the damage and authorities weighing the cost of securing the historic structure. The Spey Viaduct, also known as the Garmouth Viaduct, partially collapsed on 14 December 2025, cutting off a popular walking and cycling route. Moray Council has since developed plans to remove the damaged sections safely, while the long-term future of the bridge remains uncertain amid questions about restoration costs and the condition of the surviving structure.The 140-year-old Spey bridge in Scotland collapsed into the riverThe collapse occurred on the morning of 14 December 2025, when two western spans of the iron structure fell into the river. According to The Independent, the viaduct was built in the 1880s as a railway bridge and later became a well-used route for pedestrians and cyclists.The structure was originally constructed between 1883 and 1886 for the Great North of Scotland Railway. Trains continued to use it until the railway closed in 1968. It subsequently became part of the area's walking and cycling network, connecting routes used by residents and visitors exploring the Moray coastline.Initial inspections by Moray Council engineers suggested that the collapse may have resulted from scour, a process in which flowing water gradually removes sand, gravel or other material from around bridge foundations.Moray Council explained that a specialist contractor's 2023 assessment had found no evidence of scour at the time. However, the river's flow path appeared to have changed over the following year, potentially altering the pressure on the bridge's supporting piers.The exact cause has not yet been established conclusively. A detailed investigation is required to determine what happened and whether the remaining structure can be preserved.The historic crossing remains closed to the publicThe collapse prompted the immediate closure of the viaduct and the surrounding area. Moray Council warned the public to stay away from the damaged structure, respect police cordons and avoid climbing onto any part of the bridge.The closure has affected an important local route. The viaduct forms part of the Moray Coastal Trail and National Cycle Network Route 1, while also providing access to the Speyside Way.The loss of the crossing has disrupted connections for walkers and cyclists travelling through the area. According to The Highland Times, the nearest alternative river crossing is at Fochabers, approximately 3 miles upstream.The incident also prompted concern among local representatives about the loss of a familiar landmark. Councillor Shona Morrison also expressed sadness at the collapse, describing the viaduct as a much-loved local landmark with personal significance for families in the area. Beyond its practical role, the bridge represents an important part of Moray's railway history.Engineers have chosen a safer method to remove the collapsed spansMoray Council's January 2026 update outlined two possible approaches for removing the damaged sections from the river.The first involved lifting each collapsed span out in one piece. However, this would require major lifting operations, create considerable safety risks because of the unstable structure and potentially cause further damage. The council estimated that this option would cost more than £1 million.The alternative was to cut the damaged spans into smaller sections and remove them individually. This method was considered safer for contractors, more practical given access restrictions around Garmouth and less likely to damage the surviving parts of the bridge.The initial estimate for this approach was approximately £500,000. Council officers and engineering specialists agreed that dismantling the spans in sections was the most practical option.Moray Council subsequently moved forward with the procurement process and sought the necessary Listed Building Consent. In February 2026, it confirmed that an application had been submitted for permission to remove the two failed sections. The proposed work did not include rebuilding or replacing the bridge.However, the removal project proved more complicated than initially anticipated. The Highland Times reports that the council had awarded the removal contract to TMS Ltd, a specialist marine and civil engineering contractor, following a competitive tender process. 4 contractors submitted bids. The final contract was valued at approximately £806,000, substantially above the original estimate for removing the spans in sections.The contractor is expected to dismantle and remove the damaged material from the river before arranging for it to be taken to an appropriate recycling facility.Restoration costs and temporary crossing options remain under reviewRemoving the collapsed spans is an essential step, but it will not immediately restore the crossing. Moray Council has said that a full investigation into the collapse and the condition of the surviving structure cannot be completed until the damaged sections have been removed and the site is safe to access.The investigation will examine the cause of the failure, assess the remaining bridge and determine whether reinstating the viaduct is technically possible.The council has also acknowledged community calls for a temporary replacement crossing. Early estimates put the cost of such a structure at between £1.5 million and £2 million. This option will be considered alongside the possibility of restoring the original viaduct.Transport Scotland has committed funding towards the response. Moray Council reported that the funding included £37,000 for investigating the collapse and assessing the structure's condition, £16,500 for examining the crossing's economic benefits and an additional £60,000 for initial diversion measures. Together, these contributions total £113,500. The council has also begun exploring alternative routes for walkers and cyclists while the viaduct remains closed.You use AI every day. articles.title: From 1997 to 2002, wildlife officials released 1,550 elk in southeastern Kentucky; the herd has since grown to more than 10,000 across a 16-county restoration zone
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable journey of elk restoration in southeastern Kentucky, where wildlife officials successfully grew the population from 1,550 to over 10,000 elk across a vast 16-county area. Learn about the history, management, and future of this thriving herd.
articles.body: Between December 1997 and March 2002, wildlife authorities released approximately 1,550 elk in southeastern Kentucky. This release began a restoration programme that has since established one of the largest elk herds in the eastern United States. The animals were captured in six western states and transported to Kentucky, where elk had disappeared during the 19th century. According to the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR), the state now has an estimated population of more than 10,000 elk. The animals reportedly occupy a designated restoration zone covering 16 counties and around 4.1 million acres.Bringing native species back to KentuckyHistorical data indicate that elk once roamed the state, but habitat degradation and overhunting eliminated its population by the mid-1880s. Wildlife officials and conservation advocates were looking into ways to restore the species to its historical range by the late 20th century. In 1997, the KDFWR conducted a habitat feasibility study and set up public meetings to assess whether southeastern Kentucky could support a free-ranging herd. The agency identified suitable land and found substantial public support for the idea, thus allowing the restoration initiative to proceed.The department obtained elk from six western states: Arizona, Kansas, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oregon and Utah. In December 1997, the captures began, and the animals underwent disease testing before being transported to Kentucky. Releases took place through March 2002, with Harlan, Knott, Leslie, Letcher, Martin, Perry and Pike counties being the initial release sites.A 16-county zone with varied elk distribution The state’s elk management zone encompasses approximately 4.1 million acres across 16 counties in the southeastern part of the state. The original zone included 14 counties, with Whitley and McCreary counties added in 2004 to provide a travel corridor between Kentucky’s restoration zone and Tennessee’s elk restoration area. The landscape includes deciduous forests, active and reclaimed surface mines, agricultural or cleared land, and smaller areas for urban development.However, elk numbers are not distributed evenly across all 16 counties. KDFWR's report suggests that many animals remain concentrated around the original release sites, while some peripheral areas have lower densities or few elk. The department has now undertaken additional translocations within the state, moving animals from areas with established populations to locations where their presence remains limited, to address this uneven distribution challenge.In the winter of December 2022, one important step occurred when wildlife officials relocated 43 elk from neighbouring counties to McCreary County. The operation helped establish a new population in an area of the county that had suitable habitat but lacked a resident herd. KDFWR described the move as the final step in its restoration activities, while noting that the programme continues to manage elk distribution and population levels.From restoration to long-term population managementAs the herd became established, Kentucky introduced regulated hunting as part of its management programme. The first modern hunt of the state took place in 2001, when 12 permits were issued, and six bulls and six cows were harvested. Subsequently, the number of permits changed as officials adjusted hunting opportunities and management objectives. In 2024, the department reportedly made 500 elk permits available.The state’s wildlife department estimates the current population at more than 10,000 elk using two models: a life-table model and statistical population reconstruction. These methods draw on data used by wildlife managers to estimate abundance; however, the resulting figure is not a direct count of every animal across the state. The programme has therefore moved past its original task of returning elk to Kentucky. Wildlife managers now focus on maintaining the herd, managing its distribution, monitoring population trends and balancing habitat needs with opportunities for hunting and wildlife viewing.You use AI every day. articles.title: South African athlete Thomas van Tonder crosses 600 monkey bars suspended 216 metres above ground beneath Bloukrans Bridge, completes 280-metre crossing in 47 minutes in world-first stunt
articles.summary: A South African obstacle course racing champion has completed a daring crossing beneath one of the country's most famous bridges, gripping 600 suspended
articles.body: A South African obstacle course racing champion has completed a daring crossing beneath one of the country's most famous bridges, gripping 600 suspended monkey bars 216 metres above the river below and traversing more than 280 metres in 47 minutes and 37 seconds. Thomas van Tonder completed the Red Bull Bridge Bars challenge beneath Bloukrans Bridge on October 26, 2026, in what organisers described as a world-first feat. According to Red Bull's official report, the specially constructed course followed the bridge's arch, forcing the athlete to climb an incline, cross the highest section and descend on the other side using only his hands.The crossing tested Van Tonder's grip strength, endurance and mental resilience, even after months of preparation. The athlete, an obstacle course racing world champion, said the challenge pushed him beyond what he had expected and that the continuous strain on his hands and arms was considerably more demanding than his training simulations.“I have finished what I started. I set the big, crazy goal, and we actually got it done,” Van Tonder said after reaching the other side, according to Red Bull.A 45-degree climb at the startThe course was designed to follow the shape of Bloukrans Bridge's arch rather than take a straight route across its upper section. It began with a steep, approximately 45-degree ascent, continued over a shorter, flatter section near the crown and ended with a controlled descent. Van Tonder had to pull himself from bar to bar throughout the crossing, with no opportunity to walk or rest normally. The opening climb proved particularly demanding because it forced him to work against gravity while maintaining a secure grip on the suspended bars.The athlete began the crossing at 10.21 am with a heart rate of 150 beats per minute. By the time he reached the middle of the structure, fatigue had set in more heavily than he had anticipated. Van Tonder had expected his training simulations to prepare him for the duration of the attempt. However, the continuous load on the same muscle groups made the real crossing substantially harder.He said he had initially expected to finish in about 30 minutes, allowing up to 35 minutes if conditions proved difficult. When he checked his watch near the middle and realised he had already spent around 30 minutes on the course, he began to question whether his hands would hold up until the end. “I underestimated how tired my body would be by the time I made it to the middle,” he said, according to IOL.Grip strength tested on the descentReaching the crown of the bridge brought little relief. Van Tonder still had to navigate the descent, where gravity increased his speed between bars and made controlling his momentum essential. As the crossing continued, the tape protecting his fingers began to wear through. His grip weakened under the sustained strain, forcing him to concentrate on individual bars and smaller sections of the remaining distance rather than the entire course.In comments reported by The Citizen, Van Tonder said the incline had humbled him despite his confidence going into the attempt. The athlete had trained extensively for the challenge, but the physical demands of the suspended route proved difficult to replicate on the ground. He also had to manage his position carefully when fatigue set in. The combination of exhaustion, changing gradients and the need to maintain control made the crossing as much a test of concentration as of upper-body strength. The attempt was completed in one continuous crossing, with Van Tonder reaching the opposite side after negotiating all 600 bars.Months of preparation for a world-first attemptThe crossing was the culmination of a goal Van Tonder had been pursuing for approximately two years. Before the attempt, he trained for six months on a purpose-built rig featuring almost 50 metres of uphill monkey bars at home. The training structure helped him prepare for the steep ascent, but the actual bridge presented a different challenge because of the length of the course and the sustained effort required to complete it.Van Tonder could have attempted a simpler, straighter route across the bridge's upper section. Instead, he chose the arch, which required him to climb upwards before descending the other side. “This is by no means something I know I can do, which means it's the right challenge,” he said before the attempt, according to South African tourism agency South African Tourism.The athlete was not new to extreme physical challenges. He became an obstacle course racing world champion over 100 metres in 2019 and set a Guinness World Record for a 50-metre rope climb in 2020, according to Red Bull. He also won the inaugural Red Bull Rancher Strong competition in 2025.Safety system built without drilling into bridgeThe course required a specialised rigging and safety system. Richard Lievaart, head of rigging and safety director at Vertical Safety Systems, and his team constructed the setup with two independent safety points. According to Red Bull, no permanent fixtures were installed in the bridge, and nothing was bolted or drilled into the structure. The arrangement allowed the suspended bars to follow the arch while maintaining independent safety connections.Bloukrans Bridge carries the N2 highway between South Africa's Western Cape and Eastern Cape provinces. Standing 216 metres above the river, it is known for its bungee-jumping attraction and has become a prominent destination for adventure tourism.The Red Bull Bridge Bars crossing added a different kind of challenge to the landmark, replacing a conventional walk across a bridge with a test of sustained grip and endurance beneath its arch.For Van Tonder, the successful crossing turned a long-standing ambition into reality. What began as an ambitious personal goal became a world-first achievement that required months of preparation, careful safety planning and nearly 48 minutes of continuous effort suspended high above the river.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cyclone Arnab: 2 dead, over 50 trains, several flights cancelled; Andhra, Odisha worst-hit
articles.summary: VIJAYAWADA: Cyclone Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast early on Wednesday, killing two people in separate electrocution incidents, uprooting hundreds
articles.body: VIJAYAWADA: Cyclone Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast early on Wednesday, killing two people in separate electrocution incidents, uprooting hundreds of trees and electric poles and damaging roads.Flight operations were also disrupted at airports across coastal Andhra Pradesh, with several services cancelled or suspended due to adverse weather.The very severe cyclonic storm crossed the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between 2 am and 8 am before weakening into a severe cyclonic storm, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.The cyclone crossed the coast southwest of Yanam, near latitude 16.450 N and longitude 81.90 E, about 20 km east-northeast of Narsapur, 40 km southwest of Yanam and 60 km southwest of Kakinada, according to the IMD.Several locations in coastal districts recorded heavy rainfall exceeding 200 mm, while strong winds uprooted trees and power poles, blocked roads and disrupted electricity supply.According to news agency PTI, two people, including a 55-year-old woman, died of electrocution in separate incidents. A 53-year-old man died in Visakhapatnam district on Tuesday night after coming into contact with a live wire that had snapped over an agricultural field channel.In Yellamanchili town in Anakapalli district, a woman died on Wednesday morning after accidentally stepping on an exposed live wire outside her home, police said.Chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu reviewed the situation on Wednesday morning during a teleconference with 32,000 personnel, including district collectors, and directed officials to restore normalcy at the earliest while minimising property damage.He instructed officials to clear roads blocked by fallen trees within two hours and remove trees obstructing national highways immediately. Electricity supply should be restored once strong winds subside, he said.Naidu also directed officials to ensure adequate food, drinking water and medical facilities at cyclone shelters, protect horticultural crops, prevent water from entering agricultural fields and take measures to prevent breaches in tanks and canals.For this cyclone, the Air Force assisted in transporting teams; yesterday, they airlifted four teams. In terms of preparedness, our priority is to ensure the safety of vulnerable groups—the elderly, pregnant women, and children. Pregnant women, in particular, are shifted to hospitals or dispensaries in anticipation of the event. Furthermore, all boats are either brought back to the shore and anchored securely or moved to a safe area...People living in low-lying areas, identified based on historical records, are also moved to safer locations. Through our warning system, local agencies and authorities conduct outreach at the community level to raise awareness, ensuring that necessary safety precautions are takenHe asked officials to prepare preliminary estimates of crop damage and keep National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) personnel on standby.Trees uprooted, roads damagedKakinada Superintendent of Police G Bindu Madhav said the district had been significantly affected by the storm."Cyclone Arnab had significantly affected the district, uprooting a few hundred trees and fewer than 100 electric poles. However, no major damage has been reported and rainfall subsided after 1 am," he said.People evacuated to relief camps remained there until 1 am on Wednesday as strong winds continued, he added. The Uppada coastal road had been completely washed away, though rainfall in the district was relatively low and gusty winds caused most of the damage.In Alluri Sitaramaraju district, trees and electric poles were uprooted and some roads inundated. District SP Amit Bardar said no deaths or major damage to infrastructure, houses or livestock had been reported as of 9 am."No loss of life or major damage to infrastructure, houses or livestock has been reported so far. We are monitoring the situation closely as water levels may rise due to continued rainfall," Bardar told PTI.An old bridge in Tadiguda village of Anantagiri mandal was washed away, isolating a hamlet. Alternative arrangements were being made and restoration work was underway, he said.In Konaseema district, gusty winds reaching up to 130 kmph uprooted trees and electric poles late on Tuesday night, district police chief Rahul Meena said. No casualties or property damage had been reported.More than 10,000 people had been evacuated from low-lying areas and moved to shelters, according to preliminary information. Around 495 cyclone shelters and temporary relief centres had been set up, Meena said.Additional Andhra Pradesh Special Police platoons were deployed for clearance operations, with personnel from various departments working to restore normalcy by evening. Electricity supply was expected to be restored within a few hours, while major highways were expected to be cleared within two to three hours.In Visakhapatnam district, around 400 trees had fallen, District Collector M Abhishikth Kishore said. Roads and Buildings department and Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation teams were carrying out clearance operations, with most roads already reopened to traffic."About 100 families are currently staying at two relief centres while few others have returned to their homes. No inundation has been reported anywhere in the district," Kishore told PTI.Anakapalli district SP Tuhin Sinha said no major issues had been reported in the district.Several flights cancelledThe IMD said rainfall exceeding 200 mm was recorded at several locations in Anakapalli, Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam districts between 8.30 am on October 27 and 4 am on October 28.Kannuripalem in Anakapalli recorded the highest rainfall at 261.5 mm, followed by KVBR School in Vizianagaram district at 259.74 mm and the 16th Police Battalion area in Visakhapatnam at 259.06 mm.State government officials said heavy rainfall was likely to continue on Wednesday and Thursday due to the cyclone's impact.The Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) said flights to and from coastal Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha, including Bhubaneswar, were expected to be the most affected. Hyderabad, Varanasi, Prayagraj and Gorakhpur could also see knock-on delays depending on the storm's track.Flight operations at Visakhapatnam airport had been suspended since the afternoon of October 27, while flights at Vijayawada and Rajahmundry were suspended after 7 pm that day.The Delhi-Bhogapuram-Delhi service was cancelled for October 28.Air India cancelled six flights on the Delhi-Visakhapatnam-Delhi route on October 27 and the Delhi-Vijayawada-Delhi route on October 28. Air India Express reported 13 cancellations, mostly involving Visakhapatnam flights to and from Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Vijayawada, along with the Varanasi-Bangkok and Bangkok-Visakhapatnam services.IndiGo suspended all flights at Visakhapatnam and services at Vijayawada and Rajahmundry after 7 pm on October 27. The cancellation figures were provisional.Akasa Air cancelled its Delhi-Bhogapuram and return services scheduled for October 28, while its other flights were expected to operate. Alliance Air was operating normally, with no cancellations reported so far.MoCA stressed coordination among the Airports Authority of India, Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, IMD, airlines, airport operators, disaster management authorities in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal, and the NDRF to ensure passenger safety.Airlines were advised to follow operational guidelines for adverse weather, inform passengers about delays and cancellations, and comply with applicable rebooking and refund rules.Passengers were advised to check flight status through airline websites, apps, helplines or SMS before leaving for the airport. They were also asked not to travel unless their flight was confirmed and to allow extra time for their journey.57 trains cancelled, 15 rescheduledSouth Coast Railway (SCoR) has cancelled 57 trains and rescheduled 15 others as a precautionary measure in view of severe Cyclone Arnab, disrupting several key services, including Vande Bharat, Ratnachal, UDAY, Garib Rath, Godavari and Falaknuma Express trains.Railway authorities said the cancellations and rescheduling were undertaken to ensure passenger safety and facilitate smooth train operations amid adverse weather conditions expected along the Andhra Pradesh coast.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Vijayawada | Silver Rate in Vijayawada | Bank Holidays in Vijayawada | Public Holidays in Vijayawada | Petrol Price in Vijayawada | Diesel Price in Vijayawada | CNG Price in Vijayawada | LPG Price in VijayawadaStay updated with the latest Vijayawada news.
